extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent applicants/practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing and responding to obviousness rejections in U.S. patent examination after the Supreme Court's KSR decision, including how to apply KSR rationales and required factual findings. Covers combining prior art elements, substituting elements, and the 'obvious to try' rationale with emphasis on predictability and MPEP requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to MPEP-required factual findings when using KSR rationales
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important for Office personnel to recognize that when they do choose to formulate an obviousness rejection using one of the rationales suggested by the Supreme Court in KSR ... they are to adhere to the instructions provided in the MPEP regarding the necessary factual findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘It remains Office policy that appropriate factual findings are required in order to apply the enumerated rationales properly. If a rejection has been made that omits one of the required factual findings, and in response to the rejection a practitioner or inventor points out the omission, Office personnel must either withdraw the rejection, or repeat the rejection including all required factual findings.’’ Ensure all MPEP factual findings are expressly made when asserting KSR rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining prior art elements — consider the problem known and the nature of modification
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where a general method that could have been applied to make the claimed product was known and within the level of skill of the ordinary artisan, the claim may nevertheless be nonobvious if the problem which had suggested use of the method had been previously unknown. (In re Omeprazole Patent Litigation, 536 F.3d 1361 (Fed. Cir. 2008))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modification that merely adds an extra process step or component that amounts to extra work and greater expense for no apparent reason is not the same as combining known prior art elements A and B where each would be expected to contribute known properties. Do not treat mere presence of elements in prior art as a complete statement of obviousness; analyze whether the prior art would have suggested making the combination for a reason and whether a problem motivating the change was known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining prior art elements — predictability requirement (MPEP §2143 A(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper rejection based on the rationale that the claimed invention is a combination of prior art elements also includes a finding that results flowing from the combination would have been predictable to a person of ordinary skill in the art. MPEP § 2143 A(3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘‘If results would not have been predictable, office personnel should not enter an obviousness rejection using the combination of prior art elements rationale, and should withdraw such a rejection if it has been made.’’ Include an explicit finding of predictability when relying on combination rationale; mere identification of elements is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substituting one known element for another — teaching away and inoperability assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference does not teach that a combination is undesirable, then it cannot be said to teach away. An assessment of whether a combination would render the device inoperable must not 'ignore the modifications that one skilled in the art would make to a device borrowed from the prior art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing or evaluating substitution of a known element, determine whether the prior art teaches away (discourages the combination) or whether reasonable modifications by a skilled artisan would overcome any issues. Do not assume inoperability without considering typical artisan modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try rationale — predictability and contextual factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts apply the KSR requirement for 'a finite number of identified predictable solutions' with particular emphasis on predictability and the reasonable expectations of those of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An obvious-to-try inquiry must be undertaken in context, including: the characteristics of the science or technology, its state of advance, the nature of the known choices, the specificity or generality of the prior art, and the predictability of results in the area of interest. The focus is on whether predictable, finite solutions existed and whether a skilled artisan would reasonably expect success.
